title: Growing Up Jesus
speaker: Chris DeWald
card_summary: Chris DeWald asks what happened between the manger and Jesus’ ministry. Luke 2 shows a Jewish child raised under the law, aware of his true Father, obedient to earthly parents, and growing in ordinary life. The hidden years matter: Jesus lived, worked, faced real temptation without sin, and became the high priest who can save and sympathize.
section_intro: The sermon begins at 00:45 after an isolated prayer fragment from earlier in the service. Chris traces Luke 2 from circumcision through the temple at age twelve, carefully marks conjecture about the hidden years, closes in prayer, and leads communion through 37:53.

ledger_caption: 37 confirmed Scripture units, in sermon order

movements.heading: Christmas gifts point to Christ’s greater gift
bullets: Chris recalls Christmas rest, food, family, giving, receiving, and the wonder of children opening gifts. That joy resembles seeing someone receive Christ’s forgiveness, grace, and mercy.

Romans announces one righteousness for Jew and Gentile: all sin, and all may be justified freely through Christ. Salvation is offered simply—confess Jesus as Lord, believe God raised him, and call on his name.
Jesus lived the perfect life people could not and became the sacrifice for sin. Do not admire Christmas while leaving his gift unopened.

movements.heading: What happened between the manger and ministry?
bullets: Christian holidays jump from Jesus’ birth to his death and resurrection, while Scripture says little about childhood and young adulthood.
Chris claims no special knowledge of the “lost years.” He will cautiously consider what life may have looked like for a Jewish boy who was fully God, fully human, and without sin.

movements.heading: From infancy, Jesus fulfilled the law
bullets: Jesus is circumcised and named on the eighth day. Born a Jew under the law, he fulfills prophecy and lives the law perfectly rather than abolishing it.

Joseph and Mary obey the purification, presentation, sacrifice, and firstborn-consecration requirements. Leviticus explains Mary’s purification and the affordable pair of birds; Exodus claims the firstborn for God.

Simeon receives Jesus and praises God for salvation to all nations, then warns Mary. Anna gives thanks and tells those awaiting redemption. These unexpected witnesses reassure the parents about the child’s identity.
Luke says they completed everything required before returning to Nazareth. Every step of Jesus’ life matters because he came to live beneath and fulfill the law.

movements.heading: A perfect child among imperfect people
bullets: Chris imagines parenting a sinless baby, toddler, and child. Genuine needs could produce crying, but selfish tantrums, refusal, and self-centeredness would not.
Jesus grew among imperfect parents, siblings, relatives, and friends without copying their failures. The thought of his brothers hearing “Why can’t you be more like Jesus?” supplies the comic edge.

movements.heading: At twelve, Jesus knows his Father and obeys his parents
bullets: Luke records the Passover trip, the missing twelve-year-old, three anxious days, and Jesus among the temple teachers. Deuteronomy shows that Jerusalem attendance was commanded, not merely family custom.

Jesus’ need to be in his Father’s house identifies God as his true Father without dishonoring Joseph and Mary. Later scenes in John, Luke, and Mark show how slowly family and neighbors understood that identity.

Although the temple felt like home, Jesus returns to Nazareth and obeys his parents because public ministry has not begun. He experiences ordinary stages of growth and gains favor with God and people.
Nazareth later recognizes the carpenter’s son and his family but takes offense when he returns teaching with wisdom and power. Chris asks listeners to consider their own ordinary sphere of influence.

movements.heading: A cautious reconstruction of eighteen unrecorded years
bullets: Scripture moves from age twelve to about thirty. Chris clearly marks his historical reconstruction as conjecture rather than revelation.

He proposes synagogue schooling, study of the law, entry into Joseph’s trade, years of carpentry, and possible family responsibility after Joseph’s death—while conceding that Scripture does not supply the details.
Hebrews provides the secure conclusion: Jesus lived outside a bubble, faced real temptation, never sinned, and can sympathize with human weakness.

movements.heading: The hidden years qualify Jesus to save and sympathize
bullets: Jesus lived among real people, worked a real job, faced struggle, temptation, and loss, and kept the law in public life rather than escaping ordinary pressures.

Because the high priest was tempted without sin, believers approach the throne for mercy and grace. The sinless one then bears sin, cancels the legal debt at the cross, and fulfills Isaiah’s wounded servant.
The “in between” was a life people could not live, preparing Jesus to pay a debt they could not pay and defeat sin and death.

movements.heading: Prayer of gratitude for incarnation and atonement
bullets: Chris says ordinary words of thanks, surrender, and awe feel inadequate. Jesus entered his creation and lived human life as it was designed—perfectly.
He thanks Christ for taking human sin and dying on the cross, where forgiveness required blood, and asks listeners to grasp that the biblical life was history rather than a detached story.

movements.heading: Communion remembers the cross
bullets: Jesus came to pay for sin at the cross. The bread and cup remember his sacrifice, following his command to do this in remembrance of him.

ledger.phrase: “This righteousness is given through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe… all have sinned… all are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus.” Used to establish equal grace for Jew and Gentile.
“If you declare with your mouth, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved… everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”
“Declaring with your mouth, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ and believing in your heart that God raised him from the dead.” Reapplied as the response to Christ’s gift.
“On the eighth day… he was named Jesus, the name the angel had given him before he was conceived.” Establishes that Jesus entered Jewish life under the law.
Jesus “didn’t come to abolish the law or the prophets, but to fulfill them.” Chris applies fulfillment to prophecy and Jesus’ perfect law-keeping.
“When the time came for the purification rites required by the law of Moses… every firstborn male is to be consecrated… a pair of doves or two young pigeons.”

The woman is unclean seven days after a son’s birth; the boy is circumcised on the eighth day; purification continues thirty-three days; sacrifice is a lamb and bird, or two birds if she cannot afford a lamb.
“Consecrate to me every firstborn male… belongs to me, whether human or animal.” Applied to Jesus’ presentation.
Simeon sees God’s salvation, “a light for revelation to the Gentiles and the glory of your people Israel,” warns Mary, and Anna gives thanks and speaks about the child.
“Mary and Joseph marveled at what was said about him.” Chris emphasizes the parents’ astonishment.
“When Joseph and Mary had done everything required by the law… they returned… to Nazareth. And the child grew and became strong… filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was on him.”
“When Joseph and Mary had done everything required by the law of the Lord.” The emphasis falls on “everything.”
“They returned to Nazareth and Jesus became strong. He was wise and God’s grace was on him.”
Jesus stays in Jerusalem at twelve, is found after three days among the teachers, says he must be in his Father’s house, returns obediently, and grows in wisdom, stature, and favor.
“The Passover sacrifice was only to be done in the place God chose as a dwelling for his name.” Used to show Jerusalem attendance was commanded, not merely customary.
Mary’s reaction: “Why have you treated us like this? We’ve been anxiously searching for you.”
“Didn’t you know I had to be in my Father’s house?” Used to identify God, not Joseph, as Jesus’ Father.
“Honor your father and mother.” Chris rejects the allegation that remaining in the temple made Jesus violate this command.
“Get these out of here! Stop turning my Father’s house into a market!” Reinforces Jesus’ explicit identification of God as his Father.
“I am the bread that came down from heaven… Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?” Shows the crowd’s earthly assumptions about Jesus’ parentage.
“He was the son, so it was thought, of Joseph.”
Jesus’ family comes “to take charge of him, for they said, ‘He is out of his mind.’” Used to show their incomplete understanding.
The family arrives asking for Jesus, followed by Chris’s recalled wording: “Who is my father? Who is my mother? Who are my brothers?”
Repeated: “Didn’t you know I had to be in my Father’s house?” Mary “didn’t understand.”
Repeated: “Stop turning my Father’s house into a market.” Offered as a later public declaration that clarifies the age-twelve statement.
“My Father is always at his work to this very day, and I too am working… calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.”
“He went down to Nazareth with them and was obedient to them… Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man.”
“He was obedient to his parents… He grew in wisdom and stature and in favor with God and man.” Applied to Jesus’ teenage years.
Nazareth asks where Jesus obtained wisdom and power, identifies him as the carpenter’s son and names his family, “and they took offense at him.”
The great high priest “is [not] unable to empathize with our weaknesses,” was “tempted in every way… yet he did not sin,” and lets believers approach the throne of grace confidently.
“He grew in favor with God and man.” Reused to describe thirty years of ordinary, public faithfulness.
Repeated: the high priest empathizes, “has been tempted in every way just as we are—yet he did not sin,” so believers may approach for mercy and grace.
“God made him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”
“God made you alive with Christ. He forgave us all our sins… canceled the charge of our legal indebtedness… nailing it to the cross.”
“He was pierced for our transgressions… crushed for our iniquities… the punishment that brought us peace was on him, and by his wounds we are healed.”
“Scripture says the only way to pay the price for sin is with blood.” Used in prayer to explain the necessity of Jesus’ death.
Jesus told his disciples, “Do this in remembrance of me.” Applied directly to the bread and cup.
